speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-89, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (victims of crime), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to rise today to address the concerns of those Canadians who are often the forgotten persons in our criminal justice system, the victims of crime. We have a responsibility to respond to these concerns.
This is a high priority of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney), of the Government and of me as Minister of Justice to address this issue in an effective manner. Victims of crime have become a focal point of concern and priority in our criminal justice system. We have been involved in extensive federal-provincial consultations to address the special needs and circumstances of crime victims and I believe that the legislative proposals which are now before the House represent concrete measures sought by and on behalf of victims of crime.
Criminal Code
The legislation I will address today is only one part of the Government's comprehensive proposal for victims. Equally important is the commitment made to the funding of programs in Canada. I have offered to more than double the federal contribution to provincial criminal injury compensation schemes and to fund a new victims' assistance fund. This commitment will involve $27.2 million over three years. This is a near tripling of federal money in this area.
Turning to the Bill itself, the major effect of the proposed legislation is to enhance the capacity of the criminal justice system to respond to the special circumstances of the victims of crime in a fair and sensitive manner.

This bill, to amend the Criminal Code, introduces procedures which will ease the burden which our criminal justice system imposes on the victims of criminal acts. It will also make it an obligation for the accused to compensate the victims for the damages they have suffured.
I am pleased to introduce these measures which will increase the capacity of the criminal justice system to meet the needs of criminal act victims without compromising its basic objectives.
The proposals now before this House will, first, create a victim fine surcharge to be imposed on those convicted or discharged of offences under the Criminal Code, Part III or Part IV of the Food and Drugs Act, and the Narcotic Control Act. Second, they will allow input by the victim through the use of victim impact statements at the time of sentencing. Third, they will allow the use of photographs and affidavit evidence to provide for the early and prompt return of recovered property to the victim, and remove the need for the victim to testify as to ownership and value of property. Fourth, they will require the courts to consider restitution in all cases involving damage, loss or destruction of property, and bodily harm, thereby removing the need for the victim to apply for restitution. Fifth, they will extend the discretionary and mandatory ban on the publication of the identity of victims and witnesses of sexual and extortion offences.
Let me now expand on each of these proposals. The victim fine surcharge is one of the most important features of this Bill. This proposal further recognizes the entitlement of victims of crime to reparation, and the need for offenders to make amends for the wrongs suffered by their victims. The purpose of the victim fine surcharge is to require the offender to provide redress not only for the harm done to the victim but to the community at large. The surcharge will assist offenders in the process of accepting responsibility for their crimes by requiring them to contribute to victim services within each province as part of the debt they owe to society.
The victim fine surcharge will generate revenue to be applied by the provinces for the purpose of providing assistance

November 19, 1987
Criminal Code
to victims of crime. The work of the Task Force and the Working group on Justice for Victims of Crime, the federal-provincial consultation process, and various research projects, have all highlighted the need for a stable source of funding for victim services.
The proposed amendment would require the court to impose a victim fine surcharge on those offenders convicted or discharged of offences under the Criminal Code, Part III or Part IV of the Food and Drugs Act, and the Narcotic Control Act. The surcharge would be ordered in addition to any other punishment imposed. The only time where a victim fine surcharge would not be imposed is where the offender could establish to the satisfaction of the court that undue hardship to the offender or the offender's dependants would result. In such a case, the court would be required to provide written reasons for waiving the surcharge. Here once again the needs and circumstances of offenders have been recognized.
The proposed amendment provides maximum limits for the imposition of the victim surcharge; 15 per cent of any fine imposed upon the offender for the offence or, where no fine is imposed, a maximum amount of $10,000, or such lesser amount as may be prescribed by regulation.
With respect to default of payment, failure to pay the victim fine surcharge would be enforceable in the same manner as failure to pay a fine under Section 646 of the Criminal Code. The court would have the discretion to impose a term of imprisonment in default of payment.
With respect to victim crime impact statements, one of the needs often expressed by victims of crime is the desire to be heard, to feel their viewpoint has been taken into consideration. With respect to the criminal justice process this translates into a need to have the impact of the crime upon the victim considered by the court at the time of sentencing.
[ Translation]
Even though the courts may allow the victim to produce a declaration, this has not become current practice. As a Government we participated in projects aimed at promoting the use of such declarations. We recognize the need for the victim to be heard and that is why Bill C-89 provides for a procedure that makes official and encourages the production of a victim statement at the time of sentencing.
The proposed amendment allows the victim of an offence to describe the harm done to that person or the damages that person suffered from the commission of the offence, whether financially, socially, psychologically or physically. It does not allow the victim, however, to express any opinion on the sentence that should be imposed on the accused.

The introduction of a victim impact statement would not preclude the court from hearing the victim, if so required. The court would not be restricted from considering any other evidence concerning any victim of the offence for the purpose of determining the sentence of the offender. The proposal
outlines the procedure for preparation of the victim impact statement. It provides that the statement would be prepared in writing in the form and in accordance with the procedures established by a program designated by the Lieutenant Governor in Council in each province. This provision is intended to allow the preparation and form of the victim impact statements to be left to local practice.
The victim impact statement would be admissible at the sentencing hearing. It is expected that the ordinary rules of evidence applicable to sentencing hearings would apply. If the accused cannot challenge the victim impact statement, as with pre-sentence reports, the contents of the statement could be accepted by the court and taken into consideration for the purpose of assessing the effect of the crime upon the victim. If, however, there was any dispute as to the facts, the ordinary legal principles governing criminal proceedings would apply. Any facts relied upon by the Crown and challenged by the accused would have to be established on the criminal standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
I would like to turn now to the provisions with respect to photographic evidence. The procedures proposed in this Bill concerning photographic evidence, proof of ownership, and value of property, are intended to ensure early and prompt return of property to the victim. The victims of property offences such as theft or breaking and entering have often referred to the further victimization they have suffered at the hands of the criminal justice process for the financial and emotional burden they must bear while their stolen property, although recovered, remains out of their control.
The proposed amendments concerning photographic evidence and proof of ownership and value of property further addresses this issue by authorizing the replacement of the actual property by a photograph. Therefore nothing will preclude the early return of the property to the victim, resulting in less inconvenience to the victim before and during any court proceedings. It would also remove the need for the victim or additional witnesses to appear at the trial. The affidavit or solemn declaration that must be filed by the person or peace officer who seized and detained the property until the photograph was taken is intended to remove the need to call additional witnesses, by establishing the continuity of the exhibit until the time the photograph was taken. Attendance in court may often result in considerable financial and personal costs to the victim or witness.
The proposed amendment providing for the use of an affidavit or solemn declaration to establish proof of ownership and value of property would avoid the need for the personal attendance in court of the victim to testify as to the ownership and value of the property of which the person has been deprived as a result of the particular offence.
The right of an accused person to have the Crown prove all of its case against him has been recognized in the various notice provisions contained in the proposed amendments concerning photograph evidence and proof of ownership and
November 19, 1987

value of property. Reasonable notice of intention to produce a photograph, certificate, affidavit, or solemn declaration in evidence must be given by the prosecutor to the accused in order for it to be received in evidence, unless the court orders to the contrary. The accused can then challenge these certificates or affidavits and require the Crown to prove its case in the ordinary way.

The right of the accused to dispute any fact contained in a certificate, solemn declaration or affidavit produced in court has been recognized in the proposed amendments that give the court the power to order that the person whose name appears on the certificate, solemn declaration or affidavit be examined or cross-examined on the content of the document he or she signed.
The court may also order the production of the goods recovered when it is convinced it is necessary in the interest of justice.
I would now like to return to the provisions in the Bill with respect to restitution. One of the key concerns often expressed by victims of crime is the need to increase the opportunities for a victim to receive financial reparation for the losses resulting from the criminal activity. This has led to the increased emphasis in this Bill on the payment of restitution by the offender.
The proposals in this Bill enhance and strengthen the current restitution provisions in the Criminal Code. By requiring the court to consider ordering restitution in all cases where such an order might be appropriate the onus on the victim to apply for a restitution order at the time of sentencing is removed. The responsibility is now upon the criminal justice system to consider the victim.
In addition, the concept of victim's rights is expanded under this section. The definition of victim includes those who assist in the arrest or attempted arrest of the offender, thereby enabling the court to make the offender accountable for all harm caused during the commission of the offence.
In an effort to avoid further victimization, restitution would also be available to a person who has purchased a property in good faith and without notice not knowing it to be the object of an offence. This would include cases where the offender may have offered stolen property as security for financial transactions. Restitution would thereby be available for persons who innocently lend money on the security of such property. Restitution would not only be ordered for loss or damage to property, but also for pecuniary damages incurred as a result of bodily injury.
The proposed amendments do not call upon the court to make an involved assessment of the damages incurred to person or property. The proposals specifically limit the
Criminal Code
availability of restitution to damages to property or as a result of bodily injury in cases where the amounts are "readily ascertainable". These include such matters as medical bills, property damage, loss of salary, and other expenses.
Once the judge has decided that there are some readily ascertainable damages that could be the object of a restitution order, he would then be required to determine whether he should make the order in the particular case. He would then direct his mind to the question of how to ascertain whether a restitution order would be satisfied and to lessen any likelihood of default on the part of the offender.
This Bill contains various provisions which respond to this question. The judge would be able to consider the future ability of the offender to pay at some time within the next three years. He could also determine the existence of any assets in the name of the offender. The Bill contains a procedure which provides for execution against such assets. In addition, all or any part of the moneys found in the offender's possession at the time of the arrest could be taken to satisfy the restitution order.
Bill C-89 also contains a provision which would direct the court to give priority to orders of restitution over orders of forfeiture and fines. This provision reflects the commitment of the criminal justice system to be responsive to the needs of victims of crime. It clearly states that the victims are not to be deprived of their right to receive restitution and such rights should prevail over forfeiture or payment of fines.
I would like to deal now with the provisions with respect to bans on publication of identity. I think Members of the House would agree that victims of sexual offences and victims of extortion are particularly vulnerable to public disclosure of their identity. Protecting their identity where necessary will help in obtaining their co-operation in testifying and encourage increased reporting of these types of offences.
Under the current provisions of the Code, the judge can order, for some sexual offences, that the hearings be held in camera or that the identity of the complainant not be disclosed. You will recall, Madam Speaker, as will other Members of the House, that with the amendments to the Criminal Code adopted by this House which received Royal Assent this past June, protection has been granted to victims of sexual offences. The protection granted to victims of sexual offences was extended by allowing them to testify outside the presence of the accused. The Bill also extended the protection against disclosure of identity to witnesses under the age of 18 years.
This Bill further expands that protection. First, the protection against disclosure of identity is extended to all witnesses regardless of their age. In the case of adult witnesses the ban on publication of identity is discretionary. In the case where application is made by any victim or witness under the age of 18 years, the publication ban is mandatory.
Second, these rules are made applicable to extortion and loansharking offences where threats are likely to be made to

November 19, 1987
Adjournment Debate
victims and witnesses. Extending the ban on publication to include victims of extortion threats and loan sharking should encourage victims of these offences to bring information to the attention of law enforcement agencies with respect to this type of crime under the Code.

Madam Speaker, as I indicated at the beginning of my remarks, our criminal justice system forgets the victims of criminal acts. These amendments in my view demonstrate this Government's will to promote social justice for the victims of crime. With these proposals, judicial proceedings and the penalty award process will be better adapted to the victims' particular needs. Those changes will enable us to compensate victims in a fair and sensitive way for the physical, emotional and economic damage they suffer.
The support which this Bill has already received from victims' groups, the Canadian public and Members of Parliament indicates just how important it is. We all recognize the need to provide protection and assistance to victims of crime. To that end, I am asking for the support of all Members in this House in order that this legislation may be dealt with without delay.
1 will conclude with one further remark with respect to this initiative. I want to underline the fact that we on the federal side are moving as a national Government with respect to areas which, in many instances, are under provincial jurisdiction. It has been necessary for the federal Government, in the best sense of federal-provincial co-operation, to seek and obtain the assistance of the provinces in this initiative.
I want to pay tribute to my provincial colleagues who have worked with me in an open and very helpful spirit. I do not think I am telling any secrets out of school if I say that in the course of our discussions we have been talking about a statement of principles for the entire country, national standards with respect to programs for victims of crime in Canada. I propose to continue those discussions with my provincial colleagues and, hopefully, in the not too distant future, we will be able to come to an agreement as to the content and scope of that statement.
Notwithstanding the fact that we have not succeeded in that one respect, this initiative on the part of the federal Government is an initiative which comes at a time in the history of our country which I think is appropriate and which is a progressive move on the part of our Government and this Parliament. As 1 indicated at the beginning of my remarks, it reflects a very widely felt sentiment in our country. People who are victimized as a result of criminal activity are entitled to some reasonable consideration in the criminal justice system. It is with great pride, therefore, that I bring forward this initiative. I am asking, as I indicated in my remarks, for the co-operation of Members of the House, and I understand that
it will be forthcoming. I appreciate the assistance of the opposition Parties in this initiative. I hope we can soon go to the committee to examine this matter and pass it into law so that at last victims in Canada will feel that parliamentarians in Ottawa are on their side.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise today on behalf of my colleague, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), the justice critic for the Official Opposition, and respond to the Minister's statements with respect to Bill C-89. I will say quickly at the outset that we in this Party are particularly encouraged by the Minister's closing remarks when he indicated to the House that he has worked over the last period of time, and intends to continue to work in the months ahead, to establish national standards in consultation and discussion with Ministers of Justice right across the land. The Minister talked about the mood and desire in this country, and indeed that is something that Canadians right across Canada would want to see happen and happen as quickly as possible.
I should say at the outset that we in the Liberal Party believe that a truly just society must do more than simply
November 19, 1987

ensure that the punishment handed out to criminals matches the severity of a particular crime. If the people who are seriously injured, the victims of crime, are ignored in the process, they are in fact victimized twice. We believe the clauses contained in Bill C-89 begin the process of addressing the rights and needs of the victim. We believe that victims have been the forgotten persons in the legal system. Therefore, we welcome all those parts of the Bill that seek to emphasize the position of the victims.
As I said, we welcome the Bill. Indeed, it shall have our support. However, the public and indeed the Government should regard Bill C-89 as only a first step in finding a solution to the problems of victims. I think the Minister would himself acknowledge that the Bill is largely a symbolic move on the part of the Government. The public should be aware that even when this Bill is enacted, and it will be in its present form, there are many gaps remaining in the area of compensation for victims. This Bill will not assist the vast majority of victims whose attackers are never caught, and I want to repeat that. This Bill cannot compensate or assist those victims whose attackers are never caught and convicted.
Professor Irvin Waller, a University of Ottawa criminologist, tells us that in some nine out of 10 cases the victim never finds out who did it, and in the tenth case, where the perpetrator is caught, even in that instance there is not a 100 per cent rate of prosecutions. Therefore, the only people who can be assisted under the provisions outlined by the Minister in this Bill are those people who are lucky enough to have a day in court where they see the person who committed the crime being convicted. That is in one out of 10 cases. The other catch is that judges are only instructed or compelled to impose a surcharge on a convicted criminal if it is shown that that criminal has the financial resources to pay a fine. As the Minister pointed out the fine that can be levied by a judge is up to $10,000. But in the case of the one person in 10 who gets his day in court, who sees a conviction, if the perpetrator of that crime does not have the financial resources to pay compensation, then the judge under the clauses contained in this Bill has the right to waive any penalty.
While this is a step in the right direction, while it is a step we endorse and for which we applaud the Minister, the reality is that Canadians should not get too carried away with the notion that every victim of crime is going to be compensated under the clauses of this Bill. In fact, it is probably fair to say that somewhat fewer than one victim out of 10 will be compensated. I know the Minister will agree with that.
Most crime victims will still have to resort to provincial compensation boards to which the Minister alluded in his comments. As the Minister knows, these boards have small budgets and do not always honour the various claims. In early November, 1987, the Ontario criminal injuries compensation board refused to pay any compensation to the widow of a Toronto area police officer who was killed in the line of duty. The board's reasoning was that the widow had already received life insurance money as a result of her husband's
Criminal Code
murder. The board, therefore, came to the conclusion that no compensation under the provincial compensation scheme would be paid to the widow in question. The provincial boards, as the Minister has said, use different standards to adjudicate claims. We in this Party are asking the question: since the federal Government has now announced increased funding of these boards, why did it not attempt at the same time to have national standards set for victim compensation?
The Minister, and I applaud him for it, indicated at the end of his speech that he wanted to continue the process of seeking to establish national standards. However, those standards are not in place today. In fact, in my own Province of Newfoundland, the level of compensation available to victims of crime is the lowest in Canada. It is the very lowest in Canada. I use this opportunity to suggest to the Premier of Newfoundland and his Minister of Justice that now is a good time in light of this symbolic gesture today in Parliament to have a look at that compensation system.
Here is another problem. A Canadian who is a victim of crime in one province may be eligible for compensation on the basis of being victimized even though a conviction or successful prosecution is not realized, while in another province the only way compensation can be paid is if the offender in question is caught and convicted. The standards are very uneven across the country.
With respect to Bill C-89, we are saying today that it is a step in the right direction. It is one which we support. It is one that begins to respond to the feeling the Minister described out there on the part of Canadians who want to see some recognition of the needs and of the position of victims of crime. Canadians, those who are interested in this area, ought not to rest on their laurels, and members of the Opposition will not do that, because this Bill does not go far enough.
Last night with respect to this Bill we saw on the CBC program The Journal a timely piece on break and enters. It was a piece approximately 20 minutes long. We saw that in the vast majority of cases, almost 99 per cent of the time, no one is ever caught. None of those people would be eligible for assistance under this Bill. What we really saw is that more than just loss of property is involved in a break and enter.
Last night we saw the face of terrorism on our television sets. We saw an actual recorded event of a young lady at home alone in her apartment talking on the telephone quite hysterically, obviously terrified, telling the police that someone was trying to come into her apartment. The price she paid because of that attempted break and enter was not the loss of material goods. What she lost was the sense of security in her own home. What she suffered was terrorism at its worse, fear for one's property-indeed, fear for one's life.
While this Bill is not designed specifically to deal with that reality for many victims, this is an appropriate time to raise again the report of the Canadian federal-provincial task force

November 19, 1987
Criminal Code
on justice for victims of crime. It is stated in that report that beyond compensation the services which would appear to be the most widely needed by victims are those which help them in coping with the effects of victimization, for example, the work of transition houses, rape crisis centres, the provision of crisis intervention services, the training of workers in the system to recognize and respond to the needs of victims, and helping the victims financially where loss and suffering has been incurred.
I take advantage of this opportunity to say a few words about Bill C-89 and again to call upon my colleagues on all sides of the House and, indeed, members of the Cabinet and members of the Government, in this time of financial restraint and cut-backs to be aware of the very necessary and important role that is played by so many governmental and non-governmental agencies, many of which exist on federal subsidies and other financial assistance in assisting victims of crime. It would be a shame that on the one hand we would take an important symbolic step to recognize the needs of victims while on the other, because of constraints, we would see some of the dollars available to non-governmental agencies such as rape crisis centres and so on disappear. This, too, is important for victims of crime.
With those remarks, Madam Speaker, I offer the support of the justice critic of the Liberal Party and, indeed, of the Official Opposition with respect to Bill C-89.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, some 2,005 years ago the great Athenian legislator Solon said that there can be no justice until those of us who are unaffected by crime become as indignant as those who are. I think those words should echo today in the House as we consider the legislation which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) has put before the House at second reading today, Bill C-89.
I want to say that my colleagues and I in the New Democratic Party strongly support the principle of this legislation and, indeed, believe that it is long overdue. As the spokesperson on justice for the New Democratic Party I have called for many years now for effective steps to be taken to ease the trauma that victims of crime and the families of victims of crime too often suffer at the hands of the criminal justice system. Too often victims of crime are doubly victimized, once by the perpetrator of the crime, and subsequently by the criminal justice system which is too often callous and indifferent to their concerns.
It is because of the fundamental concern that victims have been forgotten by those in the criminal justice system for far too long, too often stripped of their dignity and respect, that we believe that this legislation is long overdue. We support it in principle.
The statistics are staggering. Each year in Canada some 700 families are victimized by murder, some, 2500 more lose someone to a drunk driver, and over 100,000 Canadians suffer, enduring emotional trauma and scars as a result of crime.
Many, many more lose their property or are victims of breaking and entering. In fact, one in six Canadian households will be the victim of a crime in Canada today. However, only a tiny fraction of these victims receive any kind of recognition or compensation.
Effectively, while crimes can have different impacts on different victims, there are four general ways in which victims suffer. Some victims of crime suffer physical injury or lasting disability. Some victims suffer emotional trauma and distress. Of course, here as well one must speak of the emotional trauma and the devastation suffered by those who are the families of victims, particularly the families of those who have been murdered. Other victims lose money or personal possessions. Finally, there are victims who suffer additionally, as 1 mentioned, due to the insensitive treatment they receive from the police or the courts, the denial of dignity which really goes to the core of their treatment.
In Canada last year there were over 400,000 break and enters. I might say that we in this House, I suspect, are not immune to that phenomenon. I myself have been a victim of a break and enter at my own home. I have suffered arriving at my home to find the house having been broken into and things scattered everywhere. Too many Canadians have suffered similarly. Unfortunately, the poorest of those Canadians do not even have insurance to cover the cost of that crime. It is very important indeed that we recognize that they must not be additionally victimized by the criminal justice system.
Too often victims of crime suffer from a lack of assistance, support and delay in the return of their property. In this regard I welcome the provision in the legislation with respect to photographing evidence and then returning it to those who have been victimized. That is an important step forward. They often suffer from a lack of basic information about what is going on with the crime. They have been shut out from receiving information. Sometimes there is total indifference when they get to the court room. The case may have been adjourned and they do not know anything about it. They have not been informed.
In one particularly difficult case, one of my constituents, a very brave woman named Doreen Helm, whose daughter was brutally murdered, was in court during the proceedings on the jury trial. The jury had recessed to consider its verdict. She and her family were not even informed that the jury had returned and were delivering the verdict. That type of callous indifference to the concerns of victims must end. Those steps which the Government is taking in this legislation are important first steps in that regard.
In Canada today approximately one in fifty victims of violence receives any form of compensation from the Government. Only one Canadian community in one hundred has any type of practical assistance organized through the RCMP or through non-profit agencies for victims of common crimes. I
November 19, 1987

am very pleased that in my own community of Burnaby there is an excellent victim assistance program which has been established by the Burnaby attachment of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It is a new program that began in January of this year. It currently has a complement of dedicated volunteers who provide a variety of services to victims of crime in Burnaby. They file up-to-date information and they explain basic police and court procedures. They accompany people and families to court. They refer to social services and community agencies. They get involved in making people aware of criminal injuries compensation programs, witness appreciation letters, and condolence letters.
I wish to take this opportunity to commend those who are involved in this program, in particular Constable Earla-Kim McColl and Constable Nancy Wilson for the outstanding job that they have done in this important victim assistance program, and to encourage other communities to embark upon similar programs.
I also wish to mention the fact that only one community in twenty-five has a sexual assault crisis centre or a shelter for victims of violence within the home. When we speak of the importance of assisting victims of crime in our society, we must recognize that, to a significant extent, women in our society are still more victimized than men as a result of violent crime. As a society we have to recognize our responsibility to assist those women. Instead, Governments, both the federal Conservative Government and provincial Governments, have cut back on programs to assist women who are victims of violence. For example, I am speaking here of women who have to leave their homes as a result of domestic violence. It is essential that those women have access to emergency and short-term physical shelters for themselves and their children, that they have access to immediate personal counselling, and that they have access to advice.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), represents a rural constituency. He has done an outstanding job in bringing to the attention not only of his colleagues in the New Democratic caucus but to Parliament, the particular concerns of women in rural communities. Those women in rural communities are particularly hard hit by the absence of basic support services for situations in which they are victims of family violence.
There is also the concern about those who are victims of sexual assault. Here again the federal Government has cut back on funding for rape crisis centres and sexual assault centres. Instead, funding should be increased for those services to assist women who have suffered the trauma of sexual assault.
We should also be provided funding to assist adults who have been victims of sexual abuse as children. There are a number of groups in Canada pressing the Government to move forward with respect to aid for adult survivors of sexual and other forms of abuse. Yet the Government has turned a deaf ear to their requests.
Criminal Code
There have been many reports and studies done on the plight of victims in Canada. As a New Democrat, I am proud that it was the Province of Manitoba, an NDP Government under the leadership of then Attorney General Roland Penner, that moved forward and blazed the trail in Canada for programs for victims of crime. It was the NDP Government in Manitoba that introduced legislation in 1986, a Bill entitled justice for victims of crime that placed Manitoba among the world leaders in assisting victims of crime. In referring to Manitoba as a world leader, I am quoting from an article that was written by Professor Irvin Waller who has done an outstanding job in pressing for programs to assist victims of crime.
As a Parliament we should acknowledge the contribution that he has made not only nationally but internationally in a variety of forums, including the United Nations in pursuing aggressively the rights of victims of crime. Indeed, it was as a result of his work, and the work of other dedicated individuals that, in 1985, the United Nations General Assembly unanimously adopted a detailed declaration on victims rights calling upon all member countries to do far more to prevent crime and provide for programs to assist victims of crime.
In a few moments I wish to talk about the importance of prevention of crime as well as assisting victims of crime. One of the most effective ways of dealing with concerns about victims of crime is to take the steps as a society to reduce the number of victims of crime. There are a variety of steps that can and should be taken.
The legislation before us, Bill C-89, while it does represent an important step forward, there is still a great deal of work left to be done. For example, I suggest that the federal Government could be showing the way with respect to policing. After all, in many cases, the first contact the victims have is with the police. With respect to policing, the RCMP could establish guidelines for members of the force to give the victim information on services and remedies that are available, as well as the manner in which the victim might be informed while the investigation continues.
The Bill before the House should be amended. I intend to propose an amendment that would require police officers to inform victims of crime at the earliest possible opportunity of their right to possible compensation under provincial legislation, and possibly also restitution if the aggressor is caught and convicted, and also of their right to make a victim impact statement to the court. Rights without awareness of those rights are hollow. Who better to ensure that victims of crime are made aware of those rights than the person with whom they first come in contact? I speak here of the police. I suggest that this is an important amendment.
I mentioned the possibility of restitution. This Bill does indeed provide for the possibility of restitution. We have to be realistic in examining this proposal and recognize that it is not likely in real terms that many victims of crime or their families will in practice be able to receive restitution from the perpetrator of the crime.

November 19, 1987
Criminal Code
In 90 per cent of all crimes the victim does not know who committed the crime, which reduces significantly the possibility of restitution. If one does not know who committed the crime, of course one cannot demand restitution. In the other 10 per cent of cases suspects may not be charged; if they are charged, they may not be convicted; and if they are convicted, in the vast majority of cases they do not have the money to make restitution in any event. While it is important in principle to recognize that obligation, let us not lose sight of the reality that the principle of restitution will not make a practical difference to many Canadians.

As was said for instance by Mr. Robert Menard from Montreal, the founder of a new association of victims of criminal acts, the Bill will even induce John to rob Peter. He has been a policeman in Montreal for 29 years. He was himself the victim of a criminal act. He was seriously wounded in a shoot-out in front of a bank in La Salle. Mr. Menard feels that small-time robbers will make the maximum number of victims. He states for instance that gangsters do not hoard money, they sell their stolen goods immediately to buy drugs or other fast kicks. Even if they have to compensate their victims, if and when they are convicted they do not have one cent to their names. Still, Mr. Menard admits that the Bill is a first step forward. 1 met personally with Mr. Menard here in Ottawa and I congratulate him for the work he has already been doing for the victims of crime in Quebec and elsewhere in Canada.

Another group of victims of crime has been bitterly disappointed at the actions of the Conservative Government. They are the victims of violent crime who need some form of counselling-psychiatric or psychological assistance. The same Government which preaches concern for victims of crime through the Minister of Justice has, on the other hand, just cancelled callously the funding which has been made available until now to mental health programs for victims of violent crime.
The group Victims of Violence, based in Edmonton, with which the Minister of Justice is familiar, is headed by Gary and Sharon Rosenfeldt, the parents of a young man who was murdered by Clifford Olson. The Rosenfeldts have said that they are horrified to learn that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has cancelled all efforts at improving the mental health response to violent crime victims.
What has been going on here? We have a Conservative Minister of Justice standing up and talking about how important it is that we assist the victims of crime in Canada, and we have a Conservative Minister of National Health and Welfare in the same Government brutally and callously cutting off funding for victims of violent crime in the area of mental health. Surely that kind of hypocrisy and indifference to the concerns of victims of violent crime who need counselling or some assistance is not acceptable to Canadians and
should not be acceptable to the House. I call upon the Government to reverse this decision, to restore funding as victims of violence have requested, and to ensure that this amount of money is in fact available.
It is not a provincial matter. It is a matter which should be of concern to all Canadians. It is about time the Conservative Government recognized it and restored this important funding.
Another concern has been raised in respect of the question of restitution. In the event of inability to pay, it is suggested in the Bill that the criminal would go to jail, would do more time. Our prisons are already overcrowded. I suggest that we should approach with great caution the suggestion that if one is too poor to be able to make restitution, if one is unable to make that restitution, or if one does not make that restitution, one goes to jail. Indeed that could lead to even further crowding.

Yes, as my colleague has just pointed out, the old debtors' prisons. There is new money going into victims' assistance programs from the federal Government. However, I very much hope that we do not in fact take away at the provincial level funding which is being granted at the federal level. I hope the Minister of Justice, in his consultations with the provinces, will make it very clear to them that he expects that the money being granted to the provinces will be put into new programs to assist the provinces in dealing with the victims of crime.
This brings me to another very important area, one which has been touched upon by my colleague in the Official Opposition, that is, the question of minimal national standards for compensation. Not only is it important that there be a statement of the fundamental objectives of this legislation similar to that found in the United Nations Declaration and the Manitoba legislation, but also that minimum national standards be established. At the present time we have a patchwork of programs in Canada. If one loses a family member in Newfoundland, one gets $9,000. If one loses a family member in New Brunswick, one gets $5,000. If one loses a family member in another province, one gets $15,000. If one loses a family member in Ontario, one gets $25,000. How on earth can we justify this patchwork approach to the concerns of victims of crimes and their families? If one is assaulted in the Province of Quebec and one's clothes are ripped, one gets compensation for the clothes, but across the border, in the Province of Ontario, one does not get compensation for clothes. On and on it goes.
It is about time that the Government showed some leadership and imposed some minimal national standards, something which it is quite able to do under the federal-provincial agreement. They provide funding and, even after Meech Lake, they can still ensure that minimum national standards and objectives are met.
One existing standard is that provinces should publicize their provincial programs for compensation. One great concern
November 19, 1987

is that that is not happening, and far too many Canadians are not aware of these programs for compensation.
I have a couple of other points to make before concluding my remarks. The legislation deals with the whole question of victim impact statements. Once again this program was pioneered by the Province of Manitoba. I believe there have been some pilot projects in a number of jurisdictions. However, on the question of victim impact statements, given appropriate safeguards and that on balance this represents an improvement in the criminal justice system, concerns have been expressed, in particular by defence counsel, that there could be abuse and that sentences could in fact be lengthened. As a committee we will want to study with care the arguments on the question of victim impact statements.
A Crown Attorney in the City of Toronto, Paul Culver, has said that in his view there is no doubt that sentences are longer as a result of the use of victim impact statements in the courts. If that is the case, we want to examine whether it is a desirable consequence.
Morris Manning has pointed out the following:
But if you go back to sentencing based on impact, you get into retribution, an eye for an eye concept. That is not appropriate in modern society.
Even the former president of the group Victims of Violence, Don Sullivan, said this:
The fear now is that the pendulum may swing too far and we become a vengeance seeking society. Rights for victims should not be achieved by denying rights to others.
-meaning the accused. On balance, the proposals for victim impact statements are worthy of support. For too long victims have been shut out of the process. As well, it is important that the accused, the individuals convicted of crime, confront directly the victims of their crime and hear personally face to face the impact the crime has had. Obviously it is essential that the judge in no way lengthen sentence or in no way include in his or her sentence the element of revenge as a result of the hearing of that statement. But I believe it is important that the victim be given the opportunity to make that statement.
It is also important, in dealing with the whole question of victims of crime, that we recognize the terrible inadequacies of the legal aid system. That is the subject of another speech at another time, but I do want to highlight that as one of the serious concerns in the criminal justice system today, namely, the very grave underfunding of the legal aid system both criminal and civil in Canada. Just this morning we heard in the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General from Gerald Ruygrok, the father of Celia Ruygrok, the 21 year old woman who was brutally murdered at Kirkpatrick House. He pointed out at the coroner's inquest that there were seven or eight lawyers representing everybody under the sun, but he himself, the father of the victim, was denied the right to legal representation.
Criminal Code
When we talk about victims of violent crime, surely we should recognize that our legal aid system should be expanded. A Tory Member opposite says he disagrees.

speechtext:
I hope that all Conservative Members would recognize the importance of the greater involvement of victims of violent crime in expanding the criteria for legal aid.
Finally, I want to note that the definition of victims of crime is far too narrow. I suggest that we examine the nature of victimization in our society today. When we do that examination, we will see that there are many victims who are left uncompensated by this Bill. What are some of the examples of that, Madam Speaker? The victims of corporate crime and white collar crime are not compensated by this legislation. The victims of a corporation that pollutes and destroys the environment, that poisons a lake or river and victimizes people in a community, receive no assistance from this legislation. The victims of a corporation which in its greed for profit produces unsafe and hazardous goods resulting in injury or death receive no compensation whatsoever. A corporation or a mine, which is not prepared to take the basic steps to protect the health and safety of men and women who work in a mine who, as a result, experience injury or death, will not be required to pay any restitution under the terms of this legislation. The crimes of multinational corporations in the Third World and elsewhere are not dealt with by this legislation. Racially motivated crimes and other organizational crime is left untouched. I hope the Government will recognize that there are victims in this area as well.
The last point is the one I alluded to earlier concerning the prevention of crime, reducing the number of victims of crime in our society. We know what has to be done. The Government is well aware of the steps that could and should be taken to prevent crime. Yet it has done little or nothing to carry out these important objectives. What about neighborhood watch programs, community and urban planning to ensure a sense of community responsibility to cut down on crime, funding for alcohol and drug programs, funding for those who are mentally ill and for those with learning disabilities? What about attacking poverty, homelessness and unemployment in our society, assisting victims of physical and sexual abuse and dealing with the question of violence in the media and elsewhere?
What about gun controls, including, I might say, an examination of the abuse of firearms by those who are enforcing a law in Canada? Recently in Montreal-

Recently in Montreal people saw a policeman use his service revolver to shoot an innocent Black youth. There are too many victims of armed policemen in Canada. So here again if we want to cut down on the number of victims we must do everything possible to reduce such abuses, such unacceptable crimes.

November 19, 1987
Criminal Code

We support this legislation in principle. We say that its steps to assist the victims of crime are long overdue in Canadian society. Certainly we look forward to studying this legislation in committee, to bringing forward the necessary improvements in some of the areas that I have outlined with respect to national standards and to informing victims and their families of what they are entitled to. At the end of the day, after having passed this legislation, there remains a great deal of work to be done if true justice for victims in Canada is to become a reality.

speakeroldname: Mr. Richard Grise (Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is an honour for me today as Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister to comment on Bill C-89, and particularly on each one of us because for a while now the Opposition Parties have been referring to victims at the third person. So I think each one of us can easily identify with the problem of victims of crime generally. Who among us can be assured that he or she will not be the victim of a criminal act in the future?
Madam Speaker, who indeed can claim to be safe from such acts as car theft, break in and a number of other infractions? 1 would not want to scare anybody but I think it is important to acknowledge that anyone of us can of course be a victim one of these days.

1 would like to thank the opposition critics who have agreed to get on very quickly with second reading of this very important Bill C-89. I hope that we will still have their cooperation as quickly as possible to make this legislation law.
Some of you may have been victims in the past. In spite of the fact that each Canadian is a potential victim of a criminal offence, paradoxically, today, in 1987, the victims are still considered as the casualties of the criminal process. Is it not a paradox which is totally out of place in today society? Surveys show that two thirds of Canadians consider that the rights of victims should be protected as well as those of the accused in the name of justice.
Is it not absurd, Madam Speaker, that most victims complain that they were victimized not only by the offender but also by our judicial system? We have all heard a victim saying that after her T.V. set was found by the police she had to wait for several months or even several years to get it back? We all know a victim who was kept waiting for hours in the corridors of a court of justice only to be told, after several hours of anxiety and several visits to the court, that her evidence was not required anymore.
Madam Speaker, many victims will also tell you that if they had known better, they would not have hesitated to ask for restitution from the offender. How many people would have made themselves known and asked for the help of the judicial system if they had been given the assurance that their identity would be withheld in order to ensure their safety?
Madam Speaker, among other needs, the victim must be able to explain what he or she suffered, and yet, we frequently hear victims complain that no one is listening to them, not even the justice system.
Therefore, I am pleased today to join with the Government which showed its interest for the fate of victims and did not hesitate to take necessary steps to meet in a fair, adequate and energetic way the pressing needs of victims.
In fact, since it came to power, this Government examined the fate of victims of offences involving property. In 1985, this House passed Bill C-18 which provided for the prompt return to victims of belongings that had been stolen or otherwise and were no longer required as evidence.
More recently, in order to assist and protect children who are victims of sexual assault, the Government introduced Bill C-15 and other major amendments to the Criminal Code and the Evidence Act.
As you all know, the provisions contained in both bills were designed to meet the needs of specific groups of victims. The provisions of Bill C-18 are more general as they apply to all classes of victims of crime. A first set of measures is aimed at minimizing hardship likely to be suffered by victims as a result of the criminal justice system.
Those measures can be summarized as follows: First, the use of photographs as evidence to provide for the prompt and early return of recovered property to victims. Second, the use of an affidavit or a solemn declaration to establish the ownership and value of property will remove once again the need for the victim to testify as to those facts. Third, the victim will no longer be required to apply for restitution: in appropriate cases, the court will automatically consider the opportunity of issuing a restitution order. Fourth, the identity of victims and witnesses of sexual and extortion offences will not be published.
Finally, if a declaration is filed, there will be no need for the victim to give evidence on sentencing.
However, Madam Speaker, it must be emphasized that these amendments in no way reduce or violate the basic rights of the accused. Indeed, the presumption of innocence and the right to a full defence are both recognized in Bill C-89.
I have no intention of discussing in detail the effects of these various provisions or the technical aspects of their application. Others have done so before me.
However, there is another provision which I would like to discuss further, namely, the provision related to restitution. Certain provisions to force the offender to make restitution to
November 19, 1987

his victim will now apply to someone who is found guilty by a judge or a jury of the offence with which he or she had been charged. Madam Speaker, I believe that it is important to take a few minutes to explain the difference between compensation and restitution.
Compensation refers to a contribution or payment made by the state to the victim under a compensation program for victims of crime. These programs are subsidized partly by the federal Government, but administered by the provinces or territories.
As the Minister of Justice pointed out, the federal Government has made an offer to the provinces which would more than double the amount they now receive. In passing, Madam Speaker, I must say that Bill C-89 has been very well-received by the provinces, particularly Quebec. The Quebec Minister of Justice, Mr. Herbert Marx, is very satisfied with the negotiations and with Bill C-89, which is the result of these negotiations.
Now with respect to restitution, Madam Speaker, it is a factor which must be taken under advisement by the court when sentence is handed out, if such an order is deemed appropriate. Unlike compensation which comes from the state, restitution is made to the victim by the offender. You will agree with me that one of the first consideration for the person who has incurred material losses or sustained physical injuries is to return to the situation as it was before the crime was committed. In other words, whenever possible it means securing material compensation for damage sustained.
Madam Speaker, this is why the federal-provincial task force on justice for victims of criminal acts published a report in 1983 and recommended changes to the Criminal Code provisions concerning restitution so that, in appropriate cases, the judge would have to consider the advisability of issuing a restitution order. The task force recommended as well that victims be given an opportunity to appear before the court concerning such losses as might be ascertainable.
More recently, in a report released last February the Canadian Sentencing Commission recommended that restitution orders take the following elements into account: first, property damage resulting from the commission of the offence and calculated on the basis of the actual cost of repairing or replacing such property; hospital and medical care expenditures incurred by the victim as a result of the commission of a crime; losses of income resulting from the commission of such crime, including those due to the victim's hospitalization or participation in the investigation or trial.
Madam Speaker, I am convinced that all Members in the House today will agree that the amendments introduced in Bill C-89 adequately respond to these recommendations.
But what exactly is meant by damage whose amount can be easily ascertainable? These could, for instance, include medical bills, property damage or loss of income. It should be understood that only damages where the amount is readily
Criminal Code
ascertainable may be the subject of a restitution order in respect of an offence under the Criminal Code. Other damages whose amount is not readily ascertainable, pain and suffering for instance, will continue to be the subject of claims in civil proceedings.
I mentioned earlier that the onus was no longer on the victim to seek a restitution order. In fact, the proposed amendment requires the judge to consider whether a restitution order would be appropriate. This means the victim will no longer have to worry about exercising this right, since in all cases, the judge will do so on the victim's behalf. A restitution order is not restricted to property damage alone. For instance, damages incurred as a result of bodily injury, provided the amount is readily ascertainable, may also be covered by a restitution order.
The proposed amendments expand our concept of "victim" to cover persons who arrested or tried to arrest the offender. However, the Bill does not propose a definition of the word "victim". As a result, the courts will have the flexibility to respond to the particular circumstances of each case. However, it is not enough to require the courts to consider whether the restitution order is appropriate. The court must also be satisfied that the offender will be able to comply with the order.
I shall now describe the procedures available to the Court to decide whether the offender will be able to comply with the order. First, the judge will be able to inquire into the offender's present or future ability to pay. He may also consider his financial status. In this respect, the judge may subpoena the offender to provide the requisite information on his assets. This means that subsequently, the victim may, if necessary, file for execution of the restitution order against the assets thus identified.
Another important detail, Madam Speaker, is that the judge may order that any money found on the offender at the time of his arrest be taken to satisfy the restitution order. Finally, in every case the judge must give priority to the restitution order.
Unfortunately, in some cases the offender will be either unable or will simply refuse to comply with the restitution order. The order must therefore be readily enforceable.
The Bill provides that the order is enforceable as a judgment of a superior court, either in civil or criminal proceedings. The offender may of course be able to provide a reasonable excuse for his default, and the judge may then extend the term of the restitution order.
Madam Speaker, the Government's proposals have been warmly welcomed by victims groups because they respond to a real need. I would like to quote the author to which the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) referred earlier, Mr. Robert Menard, founder of a new association of victims of criminal offences, who also said, and I quote:
Nevertheless, 1 believe the new Bill before the House is a first step towards
improving the status of victims.

Criminal Code
Madam Speaker, once again, I wish to stress the importance of this Bill and say that we in the House and in this Government should set aside political considerations and look at this Bill as objectively as we can. We all know that every day, people become victims of criminal acts.
Each day we defer the enforcement of the Bill, we prevent victims of crime from enjoying some direct results. Of course, crime will always be with us and they will still be victims, Madam Speaker, but at least this may help them to obtain some sort of compensation in certain areas. As long as there is no wonder solution which would allow totally and definitely to eradicate crime, we should applaud the steps taken in Bill C-89.
Once again, this Bill is extremely important for victims of crime in Canada. I hope that my friends in the opposition Parties agree and will work with this Government not on a partisan basis but with a Government representing the people of Canada. We have to deal with this Bill as quickly as possible because it does not address a specific part of the country or a specific group. It addresses the entire population of Canada because everyone, in one way or another, is a victim of crime.
I also want to express again my thanks to the Liberal and NDP critics who supported this Bill on second reading today.

Madam Speaker, as I pointed out at the beginning of my remarks, everyone of us, though we do not wish it, could eventually become a victim. It is therefore reassuring and encouraging that finally a government is looking after us and not after someone else.
