subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADIAN POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION COUNCIL ACT MEASURE TO ENACT

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador) moved
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADIAN POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION COUNCIL ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-228, an Act to provide for a Canadian Post-Secondary Education Council, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, I would like to begin by recognizing the presence in the gallery of a large and encouraging delegation from the Canadian Federation of Students who are here this week in Ottawa conducting what I consider to be a very effective lobby. At the beginning of my remarks, I want to say thank you to this delegation, not only for its interest but for the very effective way in which it has conducted itself on this topic and on other topics dealing with education this week. Those students know better than anyone else the situation about which we are speaking today. Their presence here is more eloquent than any words. What they are saying by their presence is that there is a situation in this country that must be addressed. Those of us who are politicians, whether federal or provincial, had better wake up and listen. We had better look at the situation and decide what we are going to do about it. That is what we are talking about today.
These students know that across this country today only the rich will be able to get into our colleges and universities. If you are disabled and rich, you can go to university. If you are native and rich you can go to university. If you are a woman and rich you can go to university. But there are far too many people who are kept out because tuition fees are high, and federal and provincial money for post-secondary institutions is going down. Professors are escaping to the United States. Students are coming out of college with a B.A. and a debt load of $20,000. That situation is not acceptable. That is what the students are saying by their presence here today. That is the background against which we have to look at the idea we are discussing here today.
The idea is not new. The idea is to create a national advisory council on post-secondary education. It is an idea that was put forward by the AUCC, the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada. It was an idea put forward by the CAUT, the Canadian Association of University Teachers, and it was an idea supported by the Canadian Community Colleges Association and by the Canadian Federation of Students. It is an idea supported by the Canadian Teachers Federation, and it is supported by many Ministers of Education. I would like to read what Lome Hepworth said at the national forum on postsecondary education in Saskatoon. He said he would welcome an increased role for the federal Government in post-secondary education. I quote the following from the Leader Post in Saskatchewan:
Speaking at the National Forum on Post-Secondary Education, Hepworth
endorsed what a number of groups present at the forum had earlier said they
supported-the development of a national post-secondary education strategy.
There are Ministers of Education who believe in what we are speaking about today. There are businessmen who believe. The Canadian Manufacturers Association in its latest brief said that "No step is more critical in keeping Canada competitive than improving our post-secondary educational system. Canada will succeed in today's competitive world markets only if Canadians make full use of our most valuable natural resource, that is, our people. Realizing our country's full potential demands we must strengthen our universities and community colleges". In Part I of its brief it "urges that Canada establish a national strategy", not a federal or provincial strategy, for "post-secondary education", and the Canadian Manufacturers Association expresses the wishes of a lot of large and small businessmen all across this country.
It was an idea which came up at the national forum on postsecondary education in Saskatoon recently. Dr. Ronald Watts, both in his speech at the beginning and in his summary, pressed for a national strategy on post-secondary education. He urged Canada to join nations such as Japan and West Germany in treating post-secondary education as an investment in the nation's adaptability and competitiveness, not a burden on the public purse. From this perspective, the cost of supporting education in colleges and universities is not so much a problem as it is an essential part of the solution.
This idea has widespread support in the country. It is an idea whose time has come. As we move as a country into the information society, it is essential that we move on this issue. Without education we are not going to be able to compete. There is no question about that.
Our competitors are doing exactly what we are talking about today. Japan not only has an industrial strategy and economic strategy, it has an education strategy. West Germany, which is a federal state much like our own, has an economic strategy, an industrial strategy and also an education strategy. There is a commission in West Germany which involves the equivalent of the provinces in this country and the national Government in a joint effort as partners in attacking what they know is a crucial problem if they are going to compete in the world today.
There are many people who will say: "Yes, but in 1867, provincial responsibility was given to education". That is true. No one is saying that that jurisdiction should be taken away from the provinces. What we are saying, I believe, is that in numbers there is strength. If two heads are better than one, twelve or fourteen or sixteen heads are better than two. Everyone wants to preserve provincial jurisdiction. I know, coming as I do from my province, that we guard that jurisdiction jealously. In fact, in my province, not only do we have provincial jurisdiction in education but the churches still have a historic right entrenched in the Constitution. No one wants to change that. All we are saying is that the players in the game, a very important game, should come together around
November 19, 1987

the table as they did in Saskatoon, and collectively come up with a national strategy for post-secondary education.
The reality, of course, is that while education is a provincial responsibility, 70 per cent of all the funds which support that education in Canada come from the federal Government. Why should it not then be at the table when national education policy is discussed? Why should teachers and students and college administrators not be at the table when national postsecondary education is discussed? That is what we are talking about here today.
I think that it is all the more necessary today that we involve business and industry in that dialogue. More and more there is a necessity to increase the association between the world of work and the world of learning. Never before was that linkage so important. As we move into the information society, it is extremely important that we have the people who are giving the jobs and the people who are doing the teaching talking together about what kind of education we need to do the jobs which are going to be available. That is what CMA is talking about. That is what the Canadian Advanced Technology Association had a conference about in Toronto recently. It called for a national education strategy and a closer dialogue between the world of work and the world of learning.
Businessmen are realizing that if they are going to have employees, they want them well educated, or we will not be able to compete. We talk about free trade, tax reform and supporting high technology. But if we do not have a labour force that is educated, not just once but continuously throughout the life of the labourer, then we will not have a competitive society. Thus the linkage between the world of work and the world of learning is far more important today than it ever was before. That is what Canada has to wake up to. That is what Canada has to do something about.
What we are saying is that all of those groups should come together. The people who are doing the hiring and the teaching, the students, the teachers, the administrators and the two levels of Government should come together. Why can they not? They did it in Saskatoon. They came together for three days. Is three days all we get? How long do we talk about economic policy? How long do we talk about industrial policy? What do we get for education? Three days. Is that what this nation will contribute to the discussion on education? If we can come together for three days, why can we not come together for three months, three years or 30 years? It is possible. That is what we are asking. That is what we are saying has to happen.
It should not stop in Saskatoon. The spirit of Saskatoon has to be kept alive. I wish to point out to my colleagues that we have advisory councils in Canada on the following topics. We have a National Advisory Council on Health. We have a National Advisory Council on Welfare. We have a National Advisory Council on Economics. We have a National Advisory
Post-secondary education
Council on Small Business. We have a National Advisory Council on Mining. I could go on. The list is interminable.
Recently, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) set up his own National Advisory Council on Science and Technology. I give him full marks for that. He is a man of vision. That is something that should be done. He should call those people together. They should tell him what the policy should be in terms of science and technology. But how can one talk about a national policy on science and technology without talking about a national policy on education? How could it be done? It cannot be done. One of the essential things people are saying is that what we have to give attention to in Canada today is the teaching of science and technology. That is an essential ingredient that we have to include and give emphasis and priority to in the national curriculum. How can there be a National Advisory Council on Science and Technology, recognizing the importance of that, and there not be a national advisory council on education? It is unthinkable.
Is education any less important than mining, small business, women, economics or industrial strategy? Is it any less important than those matters? If we have national advisory councils without in any way injuring or detracting from provincial jurisdiction, why can we not have a national advisory council on post-secondary education? I do not understand that. It seems to me that that is of paramount importance.
The OECD said this to Canada. It said that the lack of educational policies for the future is striking. It pointed out that there is a need to define goals for education to fit a vision of national interest. There is an array of exceptionally active programs derived from no explicitly stated over-all national conception of the country's interests. Decisions have to be taken now concerning the destination of the Canadian school system within an ordered view of the Canadian nation.
In effect, the OECD is saying to Canada, "Get your act together. If you are going to be one of the top seven, if you are going to compete with Japan, Korea, the United States and West Germany, get your act together and do something about it". That is what this Bill calls for. It simply calls for a dialogue. It is not a threatening Bill. It does not involve child abuse or environmental deterioration. It does not deal in any way with heinous crimes. It calls for a national advisory council on post-secondary education. It does not say, "We will take over the systems". It does not say, "We will throw out the provinces". It does not say, "We will fire the Ministers of Education". It simply says, "We want to give some advice". We are not talking about a massive bureaucracy that will suddenly take over policy.
The Bill calls for a 16-member committee made up of the two levels of Government that would advise both levels of Government and that would encourage research and study education questions in Canada. None of these issues are threatening. The 500 or 600 people who came together in Saskatoon recently very clearly said, "Yes, that is a good idea.

November 19, 1987
Post-secondary education
Preserve provincial jurisdiction but let us get our act together nationally and let us consolidate our efforts". This Bill is not perfect, not by any means. It should be amended. I had hoped that we could do that in committee. The Canadian Federation of Students is saying, "We believe that there should be students on this national advisory committee". I agree with that. But the students are saying that they think there should be two students out of the 16. It need not be a 16-member committee. We could create a 20-member committee, if that is what is wanted. There is some flexibility here. There is the possibility of amendment. Yes, there should be students on the committee.
The Canadian Association of University Teachers is saying that it feels that teachers should be represented on the national advisory committee. I agree with that. I think that such a provision should be made in the Bill for that.
The Association of Universities and Colleges and the community colleges will want to have representation on the national advisory committee, and so they should. Such amendments can be put forward. What I did was to draw up a Bill which recognized the two levels of Government and provincial jurisdiction. I drew up provisions for a 16-member council that preserved provincial jurisdiction since it would give the majority of members on the national advisory committee to the provinces. They have a majority, as they should, because education is their responsibility. But there are amendments that can be made, and should be made. 1 hope that if we ever get the Bill to committee they will be made. These things can be done.
I see that my time is coming to a close. I simply want to say again that I believe this is an extremely important idea. I believe it is something that must be done. It is an idea whose time has come. If we are going to call Canada a democracy and if we are going to be representatives within that democracy, we have to listen to the people, to the outstanding people who came together in Saskatoon recently. I give the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) credit for doing just that. It was an initiative that I say quite candidly was not taken by my Government. However, it was taken by the Government in power.
The Secretary of State did what no other Secretary of State was able to do. He was able to call together people of stature in Canada to discuss an issue of national importance. I give him full marks for that. I would give him even more marks if we could go further than that and if we could listen to the very clear voice that came out of Saskatoon from 500 or 600 eminent people who said that it is time in Canada now to have a national focus and a national strategy for post-secondary education. That was the message. That was the call. That was the challenge coming out of Saskatoon. Any politician in Canada today worth his salt would listen to that and would have to take some action on it.
Thus I call on the Government and on my colleagues in the House to recognize the importance of this issue. Let us send
this Bill to committee where we can examine it and where we can let people from all across the country say what is good and what is bad about it. Let them say what changes should be made and what kind of structure we should have. We cannot go from where we are now to where we want to be unless we have a vehicle.
There are those who say, "Let us go at these problems one by one". But which are the most important and which are the least important? Which will be put on the front-burner and which will be put on the back? I submit we can do none of those things unless we have a national vehicle. That is what we want to create here today.
1 know that I have tested your patience, Madam Speaker, and I know that I have been long. Let me just conclude by saying this. We are resource-rich in Canada, but the greatest resource of all is our people, especially our young people. Are we to be one of the top five countries in the world with growing influence? Are we coming of age internationally and discovering what we are, who we are, and throwing off our sense of inferiority and competing head to head with world leaders? If we are, then it is time to make education a number one priority. We have to aim at a national strategy. 1 think that that is the greatest challenge facing Canada. If we fail to deal with it, it seems to me that we will be putting this nation at risk.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stan Schellenberger (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADIAN POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION COUNCIL ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) made a very convincing argument, and I commend him on an excellent address to the House on a most important subject. 1 am glad to have the opportunity to speak on the subject of the Hon. Member's Bill. I wish to commence by giving three reasons for my address.
I am sorry that, unlike the Hon. Member, I was unable to attend the conference in Saskatoon on post-secondary education. I know that some of our Members were able to attend that conference, and 1 believe that they will be speaking on this Bill. I do care deeply about the future of our universities and colleges. Therefore, I welcome the opportunity to bring to the attention of Canadians some important matters that were raised at that conference. I sympathize fully with the sentiments which are underlined by the Bill. Like most who are interested in post-secondary education, I believe that it has a crucial national dimension that we must find better ways to express here in the national House because we do contribute significantly to post-secondary education. As was stated by the Hon. Member, I understand that this view was echoed by those who were in attendance at the forum, including the Hon. Roland Penner who is Chairman of the Council of Ministers of Education for Canada. Consequently, I understand why the many organizations, as well as the Members of this House have called for some type of national council on post-secondary education.
November 19, 1987

I am pleased to speak today on this motion because there is something very important to be said about the reason for which the House should sincerely consider whether now is the time to move on the Bill that the Hon. Member has presented, no matter how sympathetic we may be to its intentions.
Let me explain my concern by first commenting on the significance of the national forum and the opportunity that it has given us. This opportunity must not be allowed to slip away. For anyone who is aware of the recent history of federal-provincial relations in the area of higher education, the Government's announcement last fall of its proposal for a national forum must have seemed to have been doomed. I know that when the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) proposed such a meeting in Saskatoon, he felt that it was probably a "mission impossible". For the federal Government to suggest such a conference in this delicate field of obvious provincial jurisdiction would have been daring, but to feel or even hope that the provinces would co-sponsor it seemed to be quite out of the question.
Yet the forum happened. The Council of Ministers of Education did co-sponsor it. The Secretary of State and the provincial Ministers were able to look beyond past disagreements and find common purpose in exploring the challenges and the opportunities confronting higher education in Canada today. Moreover, they were able to agree at this forum that, if it were to make a genuine contribution to our national sense of direction for post-secondary education, it could not be dominated by Governments.
The Hon. Member made the point regarding others who should be involved in this discussion. Rather, it would have to bring together people with all types of interest and point of view on a large dimension. Together the Governments created the national forum committee and gave it their trust and support. Through the leadership of Brian Segal, President of Ryerson Polytechnic, the committee proved equal to the task and organized what was by all accounts a remarkable, effective event which confronted all the major issues in this complex field.
Earlier this week when Brian Segal spoke to the Standing Committee on Secretary of State, he stated that the first achievement of the forum was to demonstrate that federal and provincial Governments can work together in partnership on an issue of such national importance.
The challenge now facing the Secretary of State and the Council of Ministers of Education is to build on the spirit of co-operation and turn it into concrete action that will benefit higher education in a tangible manner. The Ministers will meet early in 1988 to tackle the challenge. We in this House should assist them in any way that we can for their success is crucial to Canada's future.
One way in which we can help them is by refraining from imposing our will on the federal-provincial relationship. We should not impose mechanisms which may not be appropriate or helpful at this time. That does not mean that this one would not be helpful, and I am referring to the national council which
Post-secondary education
is proposed. While I have already stated that it is admirable in its intentions, this may not be the time for the House to endorse it. Other Members may also wish to give advice on this. It may complicate sensitive discussions that we were very pleased got off the ground.
To return for a moment to the achievements of the forum, the event clearly made a major contribution to raising public awareness and interest in the key issues of post-secondary education in this country. Through the Standing Committee on Secretary of State the House has begun to review this field and it is listening to Dr. Segal. His view of the situation was that creating a new structure at this time would do nothing to achieve the necessary federal-provincial partnership. On the contrary, he suggested that it is important to proceed step by step in developing co-operation.
It would be an entirely appropriate positive step were the standing committee to consider some of the issues raised by this Bill today. We need full public discussion on all aspects of higher education. We in the House can help to emphasize that national perspective. Indeed, it might be appropriate for the committee to hear provincial views on some of those matters. I do not think it would be helpful to federal-provincial relations, or to post-secondary education, for us to endorse this Bill immediately, no matter how well intentioned I believe it to be.
I thank you, Madam Speaker, for this chance to comment on the future of post-secondary education in this country. This level of education becomes increasingly important if Canada is to be fully competitive in the world and realize its potential for social, cultural, and scientific development. We owe it to our country to give every possible support to developments which can encourage the two orders of Government to co-operate more closely, an achievement that the Government has fostered a great deal in the last few years.
In the Throne Speech last fall the Government committed itself to promoting with the provinces and the territories a system of post-secondary education based on the principles of excellence and equality of opportunity. The national forum has taken an important step toward that laudable goal, but it is only a beginning. All of us must help to maintain the momentum which was established at the Saskatoon Conference.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you will recognize that this afternoon we are dealing with a topic which you and 1 had an opportunity to discuss in the past. It is an issue that was raised in the New Democratic task force on youth. In that forum it was a reflection of the considered view of students, faculty, administrators, and universities that there should be some kind of structure to establish policies and goals for post-secondary education.
It is because I am so favourably disposed toward the Bill that I want to congratulate my colleague for having brought it before the House. I congratulate him as well for the excellent way in which he has presented his case. He should have been

November 19, 1987
Post-secondary education
convincing to all Members of the House. His arguments were to the point, his arguments reflected the reality, and his arguments should have determined an action on the part of the Government to respond in a positive way.
Yesterday I was somewhat saddened, when I asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) whether the Government would support this Bill to find that there was a good deal of equivocation. Ultimately we find that the Government, it appears, will oppose this Private Member's Bill. I hope it will reconsider.
In addition to congratulations for Hon. Members from both sides of the House, there has been a good deal of self-congratulation over the accomplishments of the national post-secondary forum held in Saskatoon. I must confess that I was not one of those who considered it the best way to approach the issue of post-secondary education. At the time when the Secretary of State made his announcement, 1 predicted that this forum would treat nothing that had not already been treated before and would not treat anything about which there had not already arisen a consensus, not only in the universities but among all those who have had an opportunity to consider the problems in post-secondary education in Canada and the need to have some national policy direction in respect of it.
1 would have to admit in retrospect, as one of those who attended the conference, that it was an exciting event as forums go. It was well organized and generated a degree of focus for the public in respect of post-secondary education and the contribution of colleges and universities to Canada, socially, economically, and otherwise.
One interesting thing about the forum is that there was, as I had predicted, a strong consensus on any number of issues and how those issues should be addressed. Perhaps the most important of these issues, on which virtually unanimous agreement was reached, which was expressed by the rapporteurs from all the workshops, was the need for some kind of national structure to advise Governments on policies and goals for post-secondary education. Therefore, it was a considerable shock to me to find the Chairman of the forum subsequently summarizing the results of those deliberations by equivocating about, if not rejecting, the notion of a national advisory council on post-secondary education.
Subsequently in a press conference the Secretary of State and the Chairman of the conference both seemed quite unequivocally at that time to reject the notion. We heard pretty much then, as we are hearing now, some proposal that we would take the variety of problems which exist and have been identified in post-secondary education and treat them one by one through the Council of Ministers of Education.
In that respect I share the point of view of the author of this legislation that that is insufficient, just as does everyone else. As was suggested earlier, it was not just a question of those involved in Canada having identified that there is something wrong. The OECD identified that something was wrong quite some time ago. If Canadians do not recognize that there is
something wrong by now, then they have their eyes closed. Most Canadians who have looked at the problem know how it must be addressed. Indeed, the Government seems to be moving more closely to an appropriate response to the great plea across the country that something be done.
I am sure that no one who supports the proposal in principle for a national advisory council on post-secondary education would consider the Bill before us as adequate in any respect. However, it addresses the principle. The author has identified a number of groups that I would have assumed would have been included in any recommendations on who should serve on such a national advisory council. Of course all the provinces should be represented, but certainly it is also clear that those who serve the colleges and universities, and those who benefit from those institutions, should be represented in respect of the nature and quality of education. As well, as was mentioned earlier, there is a great deal of significance in the mission of the university in respect of research and development and industrial growth. It is elementary that students should be represented, that faculty should be represented, that the Government should be represented, that labour should be represented, and that business and industry should be represented somehow.
It was kind of interesting that in the committee meeting the other day we were told that the forum was so effective that we might have another forum a year and a half from now. My God, it was imagined that we might have a forum practically every month. I began to recognize that what was coming out of these utterances by Mr. Segal was not an avoidance but a merging with the proposal before us. If a forum every year or every half a year is appropriate and can bring all these people together, surely it is possible to have something less episodic and something more permanent and more useful-a group which would consist of people who are better informed. It would be better to have something like an advisory council- people of the same representative group as exists in the forum-than to have repeated forums.
We can talk all we want about jurisdictional disputes, but we can no longer have the post-secondary system, which is to benefit the country and is necessary for our destiny, being laid aside forever on the basis of the excuse that nothing can be done because we are in a quarrel with the provinces or because the provinces are jealous of their jurisdiction. It has nothing to do with jurisdiction. We should use our imagination and come up with something that would accomplish what needs to be accomplished.
If the President of the United States can have a commission which has led to considerable reform of post-secondary education in that country without entering into the area of jurisdictional disputes, then Canada ought to be able to do it as well, and we should do it now.
There is no difference in my mind between voting on second reading of this Bill, allowing it to go to committee, and
November 19, 1987

defeating it, and having the same matter come before the committee in another fashion.
It is necessary for the Government to show a commitment to this great necessity and to do it now, before it is too late. We can no longer compromise the future of the country, of our students, of our industry, and of our destiny by failing to address the needs of post-secondary education.

Madam Speaker, I want to rise today to speak on this Bill which provides for a Canadian post-secondary educational council. I want to congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey), for introducing this Bill. He has a good background in educational experience himself and he did present this Bill very effectively to the House. He is addressing an issue that is all important to the future of Canada today.
I want to say to the others who have spoken that I appreciate the tone of this debate. They have taken the time to compliment the Member in bringing his Bill forward and put forth their own cases most effectively. As a person who had the opportunity in my earlier years to teach all grades from Grade 1 to Grade 13 with several years spent both at the elementary and secondary level, I think that the time is long overdue when some leadership should take place in a field such as this at the national level.
As we all know, education is very much a provincial matter. It is in the interest of all Canadians, no matter where they live in Canada, that education be tackled both on behalf of the young but also on behalf of those who are upwards to middle age and are still wage earners in the families of this country. Modern science, technology and developments are such that people not only have to be trained when they are young but also as time goes on. That is why it is very important to have an educational council such as the one recommended in this Bill.
If we set up such a council it is important that we have serving on that council people with vision, foresight and some good basic intelligence who are interested in the future of Canada and its people. It cannot become a board for hangers-on wanting political plums. I note that my hon. colleague from

November 19, 1987
Royal Assent
Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador has looked after that part very early in the stages of this Bill. I note too that there is no remuneration for the people who sit on the council. In setting up a council such as the one proposed, you will get the kind of dedication, foresight and in-depth interest required to tackle a problem that is really a human oriented one and an economic one.
Given the structure of our Canadian Constitution, Madam Speaker, it is extremely important that you have both regional, provincial and territorial representation on that council as well as representation at the national level in this country. The Hon. Member in his Bill has provided for 10 appointees from the provinces of Canada and appointees from the federal Government. I would suggest to him-I know he is well inclined to these things-that that might even be brought a little further to include the territories specifically in Canada.
I think the nuts and bolts of this whole thing are well laid out in the suggestion that a national forum on education be created to establish national goals and objectives for education as a resource of the nation-note, as a resource of the nation- to oversee the development of policy and mechanisms, to implement these goals and objectives and to consult and cooperate with provincial jurisdictions in order to seek to achieve the following objectives: (a) participation of the community at large, including Government, business, labour and the academic community; (b) curriculum development.
If there is anything more crucial that this council would deal with, I would think it would be the making of recommendations and curriculum development at the youth level and right across the spectrum when you are retraining people later in life. It has to include the definition of entrepreneurial and technological understanding, the necessity of excellence, and the requirement for continuing education, which I have mentioned a couple of times thus far. TRADE-UNITED STATES EXPORT ENHANCEMENT PROGRAM-REPORTED SALE OF WHEAT TO ALGERIA/ POSITION OF UNITED STATES ADMINISTRATION

Madam Speaker, on November 2, I put a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) concerning the Government's position with regard to the United States export enhancement program. You will recall that program provides one bushel of wheat out of government stockpiles for every three bushels sold through private sales to consumer countries around the world. This program has had a devastating impact on Canadian producers in that it has driven down the international price of wheat and other grains. All this comes on top of the U.S. Farm Bill which also affects the world price of wheat. Those two programs have had a devastating impact on the Canadian grain industry and that is why we hope the Government of Canada will provide a special grain program this year worth at least $1.6 billion. The damage to Canadian farmers is worse than that and more is needed, but that is another subject.
November 19, 1987

The free trade agreement initialled by our Government on October 3 said that the U.S. would take Canada's needs and concerns into account when using its Export Enhancement Program and other farm commodity export subsidy programs. Clearly the U.S. is abrogating that part of the treaty. The Minister acknowledged that in this House on several occasions. He said he would take up the matter with Secretary Shultz. He did so apparently in late October. Obviously Mr. Shultz paid no attention whatsoever because the Minister hardly even commented on what Mr. Shultz had to say.
Even worse than that, at just about the same time a Reuters report of October 20 indicated that the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture said that the U.S. will continue its policy of subsidizing farm exports in order to regain lost markets until there is a global agreement to end such subsidies. Clearly this statement, almost three weeks after the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement was initialled, indicates that the U.S. is not backing off and will continue to use this program against us in violation of the agreement. Obviously the U.S. is not treating Canada with any consideration at all. This is very harmful and makes people question whether the free trade agreement is worth the paper it is written on.
In addition, the continued use by the U.S. of its Export Enhancement Program with customers like Algeria, Saudi Arabia, Russia, China, India, and others, is not only driving down the price of grain for our producers, it is stealing away valuable Canadian markets and it should be stopped. If the Americans really believe in that free trade agreement, then it should stop this harassment of Canadian grain producers in our traditional grain markets and stop hurting Canadian cash crop producers.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Hon. Member for his question as it allows the Government of Canada to clear up a number of misconceptions which, quite frankly, have been created by Members opposite.
I should like to make two points in particular. First, the Export Enhancement Program is not new. Second, while we are dead set against the Americans using this program, it is not a violation of the free trade agreement signed between Canada and the U.S.
The Export Enhancement Program, or EEP, has, through its predecessor, the Bonus Incentive Commodity Export Program, or BICEP, been a part of American agriculture policy since it was first introduced in May of 1985. Under the program, the U.S. targets a market it intends to sell into and offers quantities of a commodity at cut rate prices. In this case we are talking 300,000 tonnes of durum wheat being offered to Algeria under the EEP.
Canada is against this provision of the U.S. Farm Bill. We have been voicing our opposition to it since it was first introduced as BICEP. We have not been dissuaded from
Adjournment Debate
voicing our opposition to and distaste of a measure which inflames trade distortions in grains and oilseeds. We have complained against the EEP in the same way we have complained about similar policies of the European community. However, our complaining will not stop this practice. Consensus at GATT to do away with such trade distorting measures is where real change will occur. We are confident that this consensus is growing and change will occur.
I should also like to point out that, in the face of the EEP and other such policies of other countries, Canada has still increased sales and market share. For example, according to the International Wheat Council, Canada has shown the largest increase in market share of all the major wheat exporters. The IWC reported earlier this year that the largest net increase among wheat exporters over the last seven years was recorded by Canada, whose share rose from 18.1 per cent to 23.9 per cent.
When it comes to the free trade agreement signed between Canada and the U.S. just recently, our two nations are showing to the world just how barriers to trade can be lowered, if not reduced entirely. When the two countries which are responsible for the largest flow of two-way trade in the world can work out a deal of this magnitude, think of the example we have provided and the impetus we have given to the other signatories to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade to accomplish the same thing on a multilateral basis.
The Americans have placed the EEP on the table at GATT. Other nations have placed similar trade distorting programs on the table, too. A consensus is forming that all nations must break down the barriers and adhere to fairer trading rules. Canada will not rest until such policies as the Export Enhancement Program are done away with.
IMMIGRATION-AMNESTY FOR REFUGEE CLAIMANTS- GOVERNMENT POSITION/STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO CHAIRMAN-DESIGNATE OF REFUGEE BOARD

Madam Speaker, a few weeks ago I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) if a statement made by the chairman designate of the new immigration and refugee board in a national paper was true. That statement, as seen on the front page, was that the Government had every intention of granting amnesty to the 40,000 backlogged refugee cases already in Canada. The Minister's reply clearly pointed out that there is "absolutely no question of giving amnesty to anybody". It is my belief that we must be able to maintain control of our borders.
The reason I requested an opportunity to speak further is that the topic of abuse of our refugee policy has been a major issue in my riding of Fraser Valley East and in other areas of Canada throughout the year. Canadians are well known internationally for their humanitarian manner, but even our patience has been tried by obvious abuses of this quality.

November 19, 1987
Adjournment Debate
When the boatload of Sikhs landed in Nova Scotia late in July, I received several hundred phone calls and many petitions telling the Government to tighten our laws. When this article came out in the paper in October, the same people were asking themselves why the Government would tighten the laws while at the same time giving amnesty to all those already here. I have spoken to the Ministers responsible for immigration several times and knew that there could not be any truth to the allegations we were reading in the papers.
Bills C-55 and C-84 have been passed by this House. Bill C-55 was passed on October 21 and C-84 earlier, on September 14. These two pieces of legislation will guarantee that bogus refugees, or those people who try to make money from smuggling human cargo by offering passage to Canada, will be dealt with by law.
As I have already said, we want to make sure that we maintain control of our borders and do not just throw open the doors for every person claiming refugee status. Many of the supposed refugee claimants come to Canada strictly for economic reasons and should not be considered bona fide refugees. When they abuse the system, fewer genuine claimants can come here.
The Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) recently tabled the immigration levels for 1988. Government assisted refugees will be up 1,000 to 13,000 and this will target refugees from Latin America, up by 200; eastern Europe, up by 300; and West Asia/the Middle East, up by 900. As well, there is an estimate of 6,000 privately sponsored refugees but there is not a limit for this group and we encourage the voluntary sector to sponsor such refugees.
The Government has, I believe, been working very responsibly to get a handle on the entire scheme of immigration, but particularly on refugees. Earlier this year the media was reporting that we were granting amnesty to refugees. This was all so misleading because an administrative, case-by-case review of each of the backlog claims was being done.
Changes that have been made throughout the year by the Government, including introducing and passing Bills C-55 and C-84, have increased Canada's ability to help genuine refugees and will continue to help deter the abuses of our system. I urge the other House to get on with the passage of these two Bills.
It is unfortunate that statements such as that made by the chairman designate of the review board led Canadians to false assumptions, but as the Minister said in reply to my supplementary question, this board will be independent and is, therefore, entitled to make its own responses separate from the Government.
In closing, I would like to thank the Minister for his forthright reply to my question and to reiterate what he said on October 29 that "there is absolutely no question of giving amnesty to anybody". The Government is aware that we must be able to maintain the control at our borders.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to expand upon the reply of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) to the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Belsher) on October 29 of this year. I would like to commend the Member for Fraser Valley East for his interest in the subject of immigration.
The Minister has clearly stated that there will be no amnesty for refugee claimants caught up in the current backlog. I am pleased to hear from the Member tonight that he has expressed that position also.
The idea of periodic amnesty destroys the very concept of an orderly immigration program. We are not saying to the world's would-be migrants, including refugees, that Canada does not take its own law seriously. We are not saying to these people that if they reach these shores, they will automatically be accepted as residents after spending a year or so in a processing backlog. Quite the contrary, we are saying that order and fairness will be applied to all persons seeking admission to this country. We are saying that refugee claimants, and anyone else for that matter, will have their cases determined on their merits, and that there will be no advantage granted to any person who misrepresents their true intentions.
The Government's intentions have already been expressed in Bill C-55 and Bill C-84 which have recently been passed in this House. At the moment we are continuing to process the refugee claimants case-loads efficiently and effectively. By early October 1987, the Refugee Status Advisory Committee had dealt with nearly 6,700 claims and the Immigration Appeal Board had dealt with nearly 900 claimants. Efforts to improve productivity are ongoing and commission officials expect to increase the number of final refugee claim decisions.
Furthermore, Hon. Members should recall that Bill C-55 contained transitional provisions by which the remaining case load under the old process could be dealt with upon proclamation of the new law. There may continue to be speculation about the manner in which immigration matters should be resolved but the Government's intentions are already recorded in the two Bills which have passed this Parliament.
CANADIAN SECURITY INTELLIGENCE SERVICE-ALLEGED INFILTRATION OF LABOUR UNIONS/ALLEGATION OF INTERFERENCE IN LEGAL PROSECUTION

Madam Speaker, on September 24 last I addressed a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) concerning very serious allegations about the abuse of the sweeping powers of Canada's security service, CSIS. The allegations with respect to abuse of those powers which were granted by Parliament in 1984, following a very vigorous debate, are very serious indeed. There is clear evidence that CSIS in its fundamental inability to distinguish between subversion and dissent has in fact massively violated
November 19, 1987

the fundamental civil liberties and privacy of many, many Canadians.
Indeed, I have produced documentary evidence in this House demonstrating clearly that CSIS had penetrated, and infiltrated democratic organizations in Canada including the labour movement, the peace movement and legal political parties. Canadians remember all too well the litany of horrors of illegality and violations of civil liberties by the RCMP security service, particularly in the 1970s, as revealed by the Macdonald Commission, and the institutional contempt for the law which it displayed at that time. It was precisely because of that that Parliament decided to create a new civilian security service. At the time we in the New Democratic Party warned that the mandate of the new service was so sweeping, so dangerously broad, as to permit very grave abuses of the civil liberties of Canadians. The Conservative Party when it was in opposition in 1984, joined in those criticisms. I remember well at the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and in the House Conservative after Conservative standing and attacking the CSIS legislation as being far too broad and dangerous. They joined in my call for parliamentary oversight of the actions of CSIS.
But, Madam Speaker, things have changed. The Conservatives have now been the Government for three years. Even if, when in opposition, they vividly condemned the CSIS, since they came to power they did nothing to change this dangerous legislation, they did not instruct the Canadian Security Intelligence Agency not to target the union movement in Quebec for example. We know very well that the CSIS infiltrated the CSN as well as the CEQ. We know full well that a delator, an informer, Mr. Marc Boivin, encouraged other members of the CSN to commit illegal acts, violent acts against property.

We have seen the abuses. Yet, the Conservative Government stands idly by while CSIS attacks the fundamental civil liberties of Canadians, Canadians who are active in the peace movement and the labour movement. It attacks those who have chosen to join a political party which may not be popular and which may be small but which, nevertheless, is legal. Surely, the test of our commitment to civil liberties is our commitment not to harass, to intimidate and to infiltrate those small unpopular political parties, such as the Communist Party of Canada, le Parti communiste du Quebec, the Communist Party of Canada, Marxist-Leninist.
We have a security service which is out of control, which in itself constitutes a serious threat to the security of Canadians. I call upon the Minister to make public the report of the Osbaldeston committee which he has appointed. I call on the Minister to assure the House that CSIS will stop its targeting of legal dissent and stop its sweeping investigations of the Sikh
Adjournment Debate
community, tarring the name of a community which is by and large law-abiding and upstanding.
I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary in responding today will make a commitment to the House and to Canadians to a public report by the Osbaldeston committee to bring forward at a very early date amendments to the CSIS legislation to finally bringing under control a security agency which is clearly dangerously out of control.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it has been alleged in the House and the media that the Canadian Security Intelligence Service has infiltrated labour organizations. I want to assure the House that labour unions are not investigated by the service simply because they are labour unions.
Hon. Members should appreciate that organizations or individuals may be the subject of an investigation by the service only if they are suspected on reasonable grounds of being involved in activities constituting a threat to the security of Canada under Section 2 of the CSIS Act. Specifically, in this regard the service can investigate to the extent strictly necessary, and I quote:
Espionage or sabotage that is against Canada or is detrimental to the interests of Canada or activities directed toward or in support of this espionage or sabotage;
Foreign influenced activities within or relating to Canada that are detrimental to the interests of Canada and, are clandestine or deceptive or involve a threat to any person;
Activities within or relating to Canada directed toward or in support of the threat or use of acts of serious violence against persons or property for the purpose of achieving a political objective within Canada or a foreign state; and
Activities directed toward undermining by covert unlawful acts or directed toward or intended ultimately to lead to the destruction or overthrow by violence of, the constitutionally established system of Government in Canada.

Activities that constitute lawful advocacy, protest or dissent may not be investigated unless those activities are carried on in conjunction with the activities that I have mentioned.
Members should note that the definition of "threats to the security of Canada" does not include labour unions or the legitimate activities of the labour movement.
Members can be confident that any investigation initiated by CSIS has not only been examined to ensure that it falls within the mandate established by this House, but has been subject to careful scrutiny to determine the appropriate level of investigation that appears to be required.
Members should also note that there are a number of review mechanisms established by the CSIS Act which are external to the service. Within the ministry of the Solicitor General there is the Office of the Inspector General. Part of his responsibility is to monitor the compliance by the service with the Act, its operational policies, and to review the operational activities of the service. This is being done on a continuous basis and nothing in the way of information held by the service in

November 19, 1987
Adjournment Debate
relation to its duties and functions can be withheld from the Inspector General save confidences of the Queen's Privy Council of Canada.
At this point I would like to add that the Solicitor General has asked the Inspector General to look into the allegations relative to the labour unions. The Security Intelligence Review Committee has also requested that the Inspector General undertake a similar investigation on its behalf.
I am sure that Members are aware that the CSIS Act established an independent Security Intelligence Review Committee made up of Privy Councillors. Its responsibilities are to review the operational activities of CSIS, and to ensure that the service is carrying out its duties and functions according to law and in compliance with all directions issued by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher). It reports annually to Parliament.
Members should also note that the review committee has authority under Section 41 of the CSIS Act to investigate
complaints made by individuals with respect to any "act or thing done by the service". Therefore, union officials have a specific channel provided by the legislation to raise the types of concerns that have been raised recently.
In summary, I would like to remind the House that there are extensive safeguards in place under the Act to detect abuses of the type Members are concerned about and to ensure that they are brought to light. I would encourage Members to take confidence in these provisions and to let the Act work in the manner that it was intended.
Same Liberal hogwash.
